title: Chinstrap Penguin Population In The Last 50 Years
sourceHeading: Chinstrap Penguin Population in the Last 50 Years

source.filename: Practice 172 - IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 2.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The chinstrap penguin has a cap of black plumage, a white face, and a continuous band of black feathers extending from one side of the head to the other, the ‘chinstrap’. The northern part of the Antarctic Peninsula, several Antarctic and subantarctic islands, and the uninhabited Balleny Islands between Antarctica and New Zealand are habitats of the species.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Antarctic penguin colonies in some parts of Antarctica have declined during the past 50 years, mostly because of climate change, researchers say. Scientists discovered that populations in colonies of chinstrap penguins, also known as ringed or bearded penguins, have declined dramatically since they were last surveyed almost 50 years ago. The findings were surprising because, until now, the chinstraps have been deemed of ‘least concern’ by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). ‘We really didn’t know what to expect, and then we found this huge decline on Elephant Island,’ Noah Strycker, an ornithologist and penguin researcher at Stony Brook University, told CNN from aboard the Greenpeace ship Esperanza in Antarctica. ‘It’s a little bit worrying as it means that something is shifting in the ecosystem and the fall in penguin numbers is reflecting that shift.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Every colony on Elephant Island, a crucial penguin habitat northeast of the Antarctic Peninsula, experienced a population decline, according to the independent researchers who joined a Greenpeace expedition to the region. Elephant Island was last surveyed in 1971, and there were 122,550 pairs of penguins across all colonies. However, the recent count revealed just 52,786 pairs—a drop of almost 60%. On Elephant Island, the size of the population change varied from colony to colony, and the most significant decline was recorded at a colony known as Chinstrap Camp, where the population fell by 77%.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The latest study was published just days after an all-time Antarctic high of 18.3°C (64.94°F) was recorded on 6 February. The previous high of 17.5°C (63.5°F) was recorded in March 2015. Scientists recorded the temperature at Argentina’s Esperanza research station, according to the country’s meteorological agency.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The reduced sea ice and warmer oceans caused by climate change have reduced the amount of krill, the main component of the penguins’ diet. ‘Climate change is probably the underlying factor, and the effects are rippling through the food chain,’ Strycker said. ‘Penguins, seals, and whales all depend on krill, which depends on ice. So if climate change affects the ice, that impacts on everything else.’ Heather J. Lynch, associate professor of ecology and evolution at New York’s Stony Brook University and one of the expedition’s research leads, said: ‘Such significant declines in penguin numbers suggest that the Southern Ocean’s ecosystem has fundamentally changed in the last 50 years and that the impacts of this are rippling up the food web to species like chinstrap penguins.’ She added that ‘while several factors may have a role to play, all the evidence we have points to climate change as being responsible for the changes we are seeing.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: However, there was also some good news, as the researchers reported an increase in gentoo-penguin populations in neighbouring colonies, beyond Elephant Island. ‘It’s interesting, as a tale of two penguins on the Antarctic Peninsula,’ said Strycker. ‘The gentoo is a species from further north and they appear to be colonising the area and are actually increasing in numbers.’

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Greenpeace ship Esperanza has been documenting the threat to the oceans worldwide and transporting scientists on overseas expeditions. For the first time, Low Island in the South Shetland Islands, north of the Antarctic Peninsula, has been surveyed properly. Researchers from Stony Brook and Northeastern University in Boston use manual and drone techniques to survey a series of significant but relatively unknown chinstrap-penguin colonies there. The results are, however, not yet available. Greenpeace has been campaigning for the establishment of three Antarctic sanctuaries to protect many of the colonies surveyed. These would be off-limits to humans.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Louisa Casson, Greenpeace Oceans Campaigner, said in a statement: ‘Penguins are an iconic species, but this new research shows how the climate emergency is decimating their numbers and having far-reaching impacts on wildlife in the most remote corners of Earth. This is a critical year for our oceans. Governments must respond to the science and agree on a strong Global Ocean Treaty at the United Nations this spring that can create a network of ocean sanctuaries to protect marine life and help these creatures adapt to our rapidly changing climate.’
